title: Is Coconut Oil Good for Stretch Marks? Here's the Truth
body_html:
Reviewed by the Real Skin Care editorial team, April 2026. Content reflects current published research and is updated regularly.

Coconut oil can genuinely help with stretch marks — but what it can do depends a lot on how new your marks are and how consistently you use it. It won't erase older silver marks, but research and real-world use both suggest it can reduce the appearance of newer ones and help prevent them from forming in the first place. So if you're wondering whether coconut oil is good for stretch marks, the honest answer is: yes, with realistic expectations. This post breaks down the science, explains which types of stretch marks respond best, covers the pregnancy-specific case in detail, and gives you a practical step-by-step routine that actually works.

We'll also answer the question most posts skip: which type of coconut oil is actually best for stretch marks? (Spoiler: not all coconut oil is created equal.) For a deeper look at the research, see our companion piece on coconut oil for stretch marks: does it really work.

What Are Stretch Marks and Why Do They Form?

Stretch marks — the medical term is striae distensae — happen when your skin is stretched faster than it can adapt. The middle layer of the skin (the dermis) is made up of collagen and elastin fibers. When those fibers are pulled beyond their limit, they tear microscopically. That damage shows up on the surface as the lines we call stretch marks.

They show up in two distinct phases. Fresh stretch marks, called striae rubrae, are red or purple. Blood vessels are still visible through the skin. The tissue is inflamed and actively changing. Over time, blood supply to the area decreases, the skin loses color, and the marks become silvery-white — these are called striae albae. That color shift matters a lot, and we'll come back to it.

Stretch marks are incredibly common. They affect pregnant women, teenagers going through growth spurts, bodybuilders, and anyone experiencing rapid weight changes. They're not a sign that anything went wrong — they're just your skin trying to keep up.

So, Is Coconut Oil Actually Good for Stretch Marks?

Yes — but the honest picture is more nuanced than most articles let on. Coconut oil works through two main mechanisms: it's a powerful emollient (meaning it softens and conditions skin), and it supports the skin's moisture barrier by reducing transepidermal water loss — the process by which your skin loses water to the air. Hydrated, supple skin is more elastic and less likely to tear when stretched.

A 2010 study published in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology found that massage with a cream containing centella asiatica extract and tocopherol (vitamin E) significantly reduced stretch mark severity during pregnancy — suggesting that both the act of massage and consistent skin hydration play a real role. While that study didn't test raw coconut oil directly, separate research has shown coconut oil supports skin barrier repair and reduces transepidermal water loss, which is foundational to stretch mark prevention.

Coconut oil is also rich in lauric acid, a medium-chain fatty acid with anti-inflammatory properties. When skin is inflamed — as it is in new, red stretch marks — reducing that inflammation can visibly improve texture and color over time.

Where coconut oil falls short is with older marks. Once the dermis has remodeled and the marks have turned silver, topical oils simply can't reverse that structural change. Coconut oil at that stage is better thought of as a skin-softening, maintenance tool rather than a treatment. If you want a full breakdown of the research, our post on does coconut oil help with stretch marks goes deeper.

New (Red/Purple) Stretch Marks

New stretch marks are still active. The tissue is inflamed, blood vessels are close to the surface, and the skin is genuinely more responsive to topical treatment at this stage. This is where coconut oil has the most to offer.

Lauric acid — one of coconut oil's dominant fatty acids — has documented anti-inflammatory effects. Regular application can help calm redness and support the skin's healing process while the marks are still forming. Coconut oil also penetrates the outer layers of the skin effectively, which means the moisturizing benefit reaches deeper than surface-only products.

Realistic expectations: consistent daily use over 8–12 weeks may noticeably reduce redness and improve texture. Results vary from person to person, but this is the window where your effort is most likely to pay off.

Old (Silver/White) Stretch Marks

Older stretch marks have already gone through the remodeling process. The skin's structure has changed at a deeper level — blood supply is reduced, the dermis has reorganized, and no topical product can fully undo that.

Coconut oil can still improve the look of older marks by softening the surrounding skin and improving overall hydration, which can make the marks appear less prominent. But it's fair to call this maintenance, not treatment. If someone promises you that any oil — coconut or otherwise — will completely remove silver stretch marks, that promise isn't backed by science. Honest skincare means saying that clearly.

Is Coconut Oil Good for Pregnancy Stretch Marks?

This is one of the most common questions we get, and it deserves a real answer. During pregnancy, the belly, breasts, hips, and thighs can expand rapidly — especially in the second and third trimesters. That rapid stretching is exactly when striae rubrae form. And understandably, pregnant women want to use something natural and free of synthetic chemicals.

Virgin coconut oil is generally considered safe for topical use during pregnancy. It's a food-grade oil with no synthetic additives, no fragrance (in its unscented form), and a long history of use on the skin. There are no known concerns about topical application during pregnancy, though as with anything, if you have a known sensitivity or your care team has specific guidance, follow their advice.

Here's the key insight for pregnancy: start before the marks appear. Applying coconut oil beginning in the second trimester — when skin is starting to stretch but visible marks may not have formed yet — gives it the best possible chance to work preventively. Keeping the skin consistently hydrated and supple may reduce how severely the dermis tears when stretched.

The massage itself also matters. Gently massaging coconut oil into the belly and hips improves local circulation, which supports skin health and may encourage elastin production. It's also a genuinely calming ritual during a time when your body is going through a lot.

For a full guide on using coconut oil specifically during pregnancy, see our post on using coconut oil for pregnancy stretch marks. And always check with your midwife or OB if you have any concerns or skin sensitivities.

What Type of Coconut Oil Is Best for Stretch Marks?

Not all coconut oil is the same, and this question trips people up. Here's the simple breakdown:

  • Virgin (or extra-virgin) coconut oil: Cold-pressed, unrefined, and minimally processed. This retains the highest levels of lauric acid, antioxidants, and beneficial fatty acids. It has a mild coconut scent. This is the best choice for stretch mark use — topically and preventively.
  • Refined coconut oil: Processed with heat and sometimes chemicals to neutralize the scent and extend shelf life. It's usable on the skin but has fewer of the active compounds that make virgin coconut oil effective. Acceptable if that's what you have, but not ideal.
  • Fractionated coconut oil: Liquid at room temperature because most of its medium-chain fatty acids — including lauric acid — have been removed. It absorbs quickly and works well as a carrier oil for essential oils, but it's not the best choice specifically for stretch marks since you lose the lauric acid benefit.

The clear winner is virgin or extra-virgin coconut oil, cold-pressed if possible. Look for minimal processing and a recognizable ingredient label. For more on the differences between coconut oil types, see our guide on types and benefits of organic coconut oil.

How to Use Coconut Oil for Stretch Marks: Step-by-Step

Most articles tell you to "apply coconut oil daily" and leave it there. That's not enough. How you apply it matters just as much as whether you apply it. Here's a routine that actually makes a difference:

  1. Start with clean, slightly damp skin. Right after a shower is ideal. Your pores are open and your skin is more receptive. Pat dry but leave skin slightly moist — don't wait until it's completely dry.
  2. Warm the oil between your palms first. Scoop a dime- to quarter-sized amount (per area) and rub it between your hands for a few seconds. This makes it easier to spread and absorb.
  3. Massage firmly in circular motions for 2–3 minutes per area. Don't just rub it on lightly. A firm circular massage stimulates blood flow, supports collagen production, and helps the oil penetrate the outer skin layers. This step makes a real difference — the massage itself is part of the benefit.
  4. Focus on high-risk areas. During pregnancy: belly, hips, thighs, breasts. During growth or weight changes: upper arms, inner thighs, lower back. Apply wherever your skin is actively stretching.
  5. Apply once or twice daily. Morning and evening is ideal. Once daily is acceptable if that's what fits your routine.
  6. Be consistent for at least 8–12 weeks. This is non-negotiable. Occasional use won't produce results. Set a reminder if you need to — this works through repetition.
  7. Layer with a body lotion if you want longer-lasting moisture. Applying a body lotion over the top can help seal in the coconut oil and extend hydration throughout the day. If you'd rather skip the two-step routine, a coconut oil body lotion combines both in one step — more on that in a moment.

If raw oil feels too heavy or greasy for your routine, a well-formulated coconut oil body lotion gives you the same skin benefits in a lighter, ready-to-use format that absorbs more easily. See our guide to coconut oil body lotions for dry skin for options.

Benefits of Coconut Oil for Skin Beyond Stretch Marks

Coconut oil earns its reputation as a skin ingredient for reasons that go well beyond stretch marks. Understanding why it works for your skin in general helps explain why it's so useful for prevention and repair. For a full deep-dive, see our post on coconut oil as a moisturizer for skin.

  • Deep moisturization: Coconut oil works as both an emollient (softens skin cells) and an occlusive (seals moisture in). That two-layer hydration is part of why it's so effective on dry or stretched skin.
  • Anti-inflammatory support: Lauric acid has documented anti-inflammatory properties, which is why coconut oil can visibly calm redness in newer stretch marks and reactive skin generally.
  • Antimicrobial properties: Lauric acid also has antimicrobial effects, which supports overall skin health and may reduce the risk of minor surface infections on compromised skin.
  • Antioxidant content: Virgin coconut oil contains vitamin E and polyphenols — compounds that help protect skin cells from oxidative stress and environmental damage.
  • Skin barrier support: Research has shown coconut oil reduces transepidermal water loss, which means it helps your skin hold onto moisture more effectively over time — not just in the short term.

These benefits work together, which is why consistent use of coconut oil on the skin has a compounding effect that's hard to replicate with a single-function product.

Are There Any Risks or Side Effects?

Coconut oil is very well tolerated by most people — but it's worth knowing a few things before you start. For a full overview of coconut oil's skin profile, our post on coconut oil for skin: benefits and potential downsides covers everything.

  • It's comedogenic on the face: Coconut oil has a comedogenic rating of 4 out of 5, which means it can clog pores and cause breakouts — particularly on facial skin. For stretch marks on the belly, thighs, or hips, this is rarely a concern since those areas aren't acne-prone. Just don't use it on your face.
  • Patch test if you have sensitive skin: Apply a small amount to the inside of your wrist and wait 24 hours before using it on larger areas. This is especially worth doing if you have a known tree nut sensitivity.
  • May not suit very oily skin: If your skin tends to be oily, a lighter coconut oil lotion formulation may be more comfortable than raw oil applied directly.
  • Generally safe for most people: If you're applying it to the belly, thighs, or hips for stretch mark purposes, the vast majority of people will have no issues at all.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is coconut oil good for stretch marks on the stomach?
Yes — the stomach is actually one of the best areas to use it, especially during pregnancy or periods of weight change when the skin is actively stretching. Starting before visible marks appear gives you the best preventive benefit. Apply after showering and massage in circular motions for a few minutes.

How long does it take for coconut oil to work on stretch marks?
Expect 8–12 weeks of consistent daily use before you see meaningful changes in texture or color. Newer, red marks respond faster than older, silver ones. Skipping days slows results significantly — consistency is the most important factor.

Can I use coconut oil for stretch marks every day?
Yes, and you should. Daily application is both safe and recommended for most skin types. Once a day is a minimum; twice daily (morning and evening) will produce better results over time.

Is virgin coconut oil better than refined coconut oil for stretch marks?
Yes. Virgin coconut oil retains more lauric acid, antioxidants, and beneficial fatty acids than refined versions. Those compounds are part of what makes it effective for skin hydration and inflammation. When buying specifically for skin use, look for cold-pressed, unrefined, virgin or extra-virgin on the label.

Does coconut oil actually remove stretch marks?
No — and any product that claims to fully remove stretch marks is overpromising. Coconut oil can improve the appearance of stretch marks, especially newer ones, and may help prevent new ones from forming. But older, silver marks represent a structural change in the dermis that topical oils cannot reverse. What coconut oil can do is make your skin visibly healthier, softer, and more hydrated — which matters.
